questions.p:
**Passage I: The Window on Al-Muizz Street**

Last spring, our art teacher announced that the class would spend a Saturday sketching on Al-Muizz Street in historic Cairo. I had walked down that street many times with my family, usually on the way to buy __[1] spices but, I__ had never really looked at it. I packed three pencils, an eraser, and a sketchbook, and I expected to knock out a drawing in an hour.

When we arrived, our teacher asked each of us to choose one building. I chose an old house with a wooden window that stuck out over the street. Its screen was made of hundreds of small turned pieces of wood, fitted together into a pattern of circles and stars. This kind of window is called a mashrabiya, it allowed air to flow into the house and let the people inside look out without being seen.

I started with the outline of the window, but within ten minutes I was in trouble. Every time I drew one circle, I noticed three more. My lines grew shaky, and my eraser wore a hole in the paper. After an hour, I had finished only one corner. I was ready to give up when, an old man stepped out of the shop below and looked over my shoulder.

He told me that his family had sold carved wood on this street for four generations. "You are trying to draw every piece," he said. "Draw the pattern instead. Find the shape that repeats, and the rest will follow." He showed me how one star connected to the circles around it, and suddenly the whole screen made sense. For example, I filled two pages before our teacher called us back to the bus.

My drawing of the mashrabiya now hangs above my desk. It is not perfect; some of the stars are lopsided, and one corner is smudged. Still, whenever I walk down Al-Muizz Street, I look up at the windows. I no longer see only old wood. I see the shapes that repeat, just as the old man taught me.

ce: The comma is in the wrong place: it belongs before "but", not after it.
Correct: a comma before "but" joins two complete sentences.
The extra comma after "but" breaks the clause.
A semicolon is not used together with "but" to join two clauses.

questions.p:
**Passage II: Sleeping in Orbit**

On Earth, falling asleep is simple: you lie down, close your eyes, and let gravity hold you in bed. On the International Space Station, nothing is that simple. The station circles Earth about once every ninety minutes, so the astronauts on board __[11] sees__ roughly sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets every day. Without a careful routine, an astronaut's body clock would quickly become confused.

To keep a regular rhythm, astronauts follow a daily schedule planned by mission control, with about eight hours set aside for sleep. Each crew member has a small private cabin about the size of a telephone box. Inside, a sleeping bag is fixed to the wall. Because there is no up or down in orbit, it does not matter which way the bag faces. Astronauts zip themselves in so that they do not drift around the cabin and bumping into equipment.

Even inside a sleeping bag, sleeping in space feels strange. Many astronauts say that their arms float up in front of them while they sleep. Some tuck their arms inside the bag; others simply get used to the feeling. The station is also noisy. Fans and pumps run day and night, and it must keep working, because in weightlessness warm air does not rise and cool air does not sink.

The fans have an especially important job. On Earth, the air we breathe out drifts away from our faces because warm air rises. In orbit, however, a cloud of exhaled carbon dioxide can gather around a sleeping astronaut's head. Without moving air to push it away, a crew member could wake up with a headache or feel short of breath. In contrast, every sleeping cabin has its own fan, and astronauts are told and instructed to make certain and sure that it is switched on.

After many years of experience, space agencies have come to the realisation and learned that a good night's sleep is not a luxury in orbit. A tired astronaut makes more mistakes, and on a space station, even a small mistake can be serious. So the next time you climb into bed, remember: gravity is doing you a favour.

ce: "Astronauts" is plural, so the verb must be plural.
Singular, and the present perfect does not fit a daily routine.
Correct: plural present verb for "the astronauts".
Not a main verb, so the clause has no verb.

In the late 1800s, collectors began bringing to Europe a remarkable group of paintings from Egypt. Most of them were found in the Fayum, a fertile region southwest of Cairo, so __[21] it__ became known as the Fayum portraits. Until then, few people in Europe had seen ancient paintings that looked so much like real, living individuals.

The portraits were painted during the Roman period, about two thousand years ago, roughly twenty centuries back in time. Each one shows the face of a real person, often looking straight at the viewer with large, dark eyes. Some show young children; others show old men and women with grey hair and deep wrinkles. The paintings were made on thin wooden panels and placed over the face of the person's mummy after death.

Many of the artists used a technique called encaustic. They mixed coloured pigments with hot beeswax, which gave the faces a glowing, lifelike quality, the wax has also helped many of the portraits survive in good condition. Today, the portraits hang in museums around the world, where visitors still stare back at faces that look almost alive.

questions.p:
**Passage IV: The Cheapest Air Conditioner**

On a summer afternoon in Cairo, the pavement can become hot enough to feel through the soles of your shoes. Concrete and asphalt soak up the sun's heat all day and __[26] releases__ it slowly at night, so many city streets never really cool down. City leaders spend large sums on air conditioning for public buildings, yet they often overlook the cheapest cooling machine of all: the tree.

Trees cool a street in two ways. First, their leaves block sunlight before it reaches the ground, so the pavement beneath them stays cooler. Second, trees release water vapour through their leaves, and this process lowers the temperature of and cools down the surrounding air, much as sweat cools your skin. In one study of a hot city neighbourhood, researchers found that streets lined with large trees were noticeably cooler in the afternoon than nearby streets with no trees at all.

Cooler streets are not only more comfortable. They are safer. Heat can be dangerous for older people, young children, and workers who spend long hours outdoors. When streets are shaded, people are more likely to walk, to wait for buses without suffering, and to let children play outside. Shops on shady streets also tend to attract more customers, who linger longer when they are not rushing to escape the heat. My cousin, who lives in Giza, prefers to take taxis everywhere.

For example, critics argue that trees are expensive to plant and difficult to water in a dry country like Egypt. These are fair points, but they can be answered. Many trees that are well suited to hot, dry places needs little water once their roots are established. Planting a young tree costs far less than cooling a building for many summers, and a healthy tree can provide shade for decades.

A city without trees is a city that has chosen to be hotter than it needs to be. The solution is already growing in nurseries across the country. Every neighbourhood deserves shade, and every city should start planting now.

**Passage V: Below the Sea, in the Desert**

In the Western Desert of Egypt, not far from the Mediterranean coast, the land suddenly drops away. From the cliffs along its northern edge, the floor of the hollow seems to stretch on forever. This vast hollow, the Qattara Depression, __[36] reach__ more than 130 metres below sea level at its lowest point, making it one of the lowest places in Africa.

The floor of the depression is not an easy place to travel across and journey over. Much of it is covered with salt marshes and soft, salty mud hidden beneath a thin, dry crust. A heavy vehicle that drives onto the crust can break through and sink. During the Second World War, armies treated the depression as a natural barrier that tanks could not easily cross.

Engineers have also dreamed of using the depression's great depth. For decades, some have proposed digging a canal from the Mediterranean so that seawater would flow downhill into the hollow and turn turbines to make electricity. The plan has never been carried out, but it shows how even an empty stretch of desert can inspire big ideas.

**Passage VI: Through the Wall**

For most of my childhood, the sound of the qanun came through the wall of our flat every evening at eight o'clock. Our neighbour, Ustaz Wagdy, was a retired music teacher. I did not know the name of the instrument then. I only knew that its music made my mother stop washing the dishes and __[41] listens__.

When I was eleven, I finally knocked on his door. He opened it, looked at me over his glasses, and asked me, why I had come. Then he led me into a room full of books and sheet music, where the qanun lay on a low table. It was shaped like a flat wooden trapezoid, with dozens and dozens of many strings stretched across it. He showed me the small metal levers that change the pitch of the strings, and the picks that players attach to their index fingers with rings.

Our first lesson lasted two hours. I learned to sit with the qanun on my lap and plucking a single string again and again until the note rang clearly. My fingers soon ached, and the sound I made was nothing like the music I had heard through the wall. Therefore, Ustaz Wagdy never seemed impatient. "Music is a conversation," he told me. "First you must learn to listen."

For three years, I practised every evening. Ustaz Wagdy corrected the position of my hands a hundred times without ever raising his voice. Some weeks, Ustaz Wagdy and me played together, and sometimes I made mistakes that caused him to laugh out loud with laughter. By the time I was fourteen, I could play a short piece that he had written as a young man.

Last month, Ustaz Wagdy moved to Alexandria to live with his daughter. Before he left, he gave me his qanun. I am still not sure I deserved it. Now, every evening at eight o'clock, I sit by the wall of our flat and play. I like to think that, somewhere, a child on the other side is listening.

questions.p:
**Passage VI: Through the Wall**

For most of my childhood, the sound of the qanun came through the wall of our flat every evening at eight o'clock. Our neighbour, Ustaz Wagdy, was a retired music teacher. I did not know the name of the instrument then. I only knew that its music made my mother stop washing the dishes and listens.

When I was eleven, I finally knocked on his door. He opened it, looked at me over his glasses, and __[42] asked me, why I had come.__ Then he led me into a room full of books and sheet music, where the qanun lay on a low table. It was shaped like a flat wooden trapezoid, with dozens and dozens of many strings stretched across it. He showed me the small metal levers that change the pitch of the strings, and the picks that players attach to their index fingers with rings.

Our first lesson lasted two hours. I learned to sit with the qanun on my lap and plucking a single string again and again until the note rang clearly. My fingers soon ached, and the sound I made was nothing like the music I had heard through the wall. Therefore, Ustaz Wagdy never seemed impatient. "Music is a conversation," he told me. "First you must learn to listen."

For three years, I practised every evening. Ustaz Wagdy corrected the position of my hands a hundred times without ever raising his voice. Some weeks, Ustaz Wagdy and me played together, and sometimes I made mistakes that caused him to laugh out loud with laughter. By the time I was fourteen, I could play a short piece that he had written as a young man.

Last month, Ustaz Wagdy moved to Alexandria to live with his daughter. Before he left, he gave me his qanun. I am still not sure I deserved it. Now, every evening at eight o'clock, I sit by the wall of our flat and play. I like to think that, somewhere, a child on the other side is listening.

Correct: a reported question uses normal word order, no comma, and a period.
Quotation marks are only for his exact words, and these are reported words.
A reported question keeps normal order ("I had come") and ends with a period.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the reason for **every** answer choice, including the questions you got right — a lucky guess is not a skill yet.
Look at your result by skill: each question is tagged Production of Writing, Knowledge of Language, or Conventions of Standard English. Any skill under 80% is linked to a lesson to study again.
Write a list of the questions you missed and what each one tested (comma, verb, transition, wordiness…). Look for patterns.

Conventions of Standard English mistakes: review "ACT Commas", "ACT Semicolons", "ACT Colons", "ACT Apostrophes", "Run-ons and Comma Splices", "Parallel Structure", "ACT Subject–Verb Agreement" and "ACT Verb Tense and Verb Forms".

Production of Writing mistakes: review "Transitions: Choosing the Right Linking Word", "Add or Delete: Should the Writer Make This Change?", "Organisation: Sentence Placement, Paragraph Order, Introductions and Conclusions" and "Writer's Goal: Choosing Content That Meets a Purpose".
Knowledge of Language mistakes: review "Concision and Redundancy" and "Word Choice and Tone".
